title: Keir Starmer Donates His Own Biography to Historic Downing Street Library
author: Sarah Jenkins
image: /images/news/Starmer Donates Biography of Himself to Downing Street Library.webp
excerpt: Former UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has donated a biography about himself, written by former Labour adviser Tom Baldwin, to the historic Downing Street library.

content.text: Former UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has donated a biography about himself to the historic library at Downing Street, adding an unusual personal item to a collection built over decades by British prime ministers and government ministers. The book, Keir Starmer: The Biography, was written by journalist and former Labour adviser Tom Baldwin and has now joined the collection of more than 400 books housed in the Cabinet Room area of 10 Downing Street. The donation comes as Starmer's political career enters a new phase following his decision to step down as prime minister, giving the addition an unusual historical significance.

The Downing Street library is not an ordinary government library. It has developed over many decades into a collection reflecting the interests, political careers and personal tastes of Britain's leaders. The tradition dates back to 1931, when Labour Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald established the collection. Since then, successive prime ministers and ministers have contributed books covering politics, history, philosophy, religion, literature, culture and even personal interests. The collection has therefore become a small record of the people who have occupied some of the most powerful positions in British government.

Starmer's choice is likely to attract attention because the donated book is not simply about British politics or a historical figure — it is a biography of Starmer himself. Written by Baldwin, a former Labour adviser who worked closely with Starmer, the biography examines his background, political rise and transformation of the Labour Party. By placing a copy in the Downing Street library, the book will sit alongside works connected to previous prime ministers and political figures, effectively making Starmer himself part of the library's historical record.

The donation is also part of a wider contribution from members of Starmer's former government. Several ministers donated books to the collection, creating a snapshot of the interests and political influences of the Labour administration. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, for example, donated a book about the political life of Alice Bacon, while other ministers contributed works dealing with Catholic social teaching, democratic socialism, Harold Wilson, Welsh mining history and public-sector reform. The range of titles demonstrates that the Downing Street collection is not limited to conventional political memoirs and biographies.

The timing of Starmer's donation adds another layer to the story. He became prime minister after Labour's victory in the 2024 general election, ending 14 years of Conservative-led governments. His administration subsequently faced a series of political and economic challenges, including pressure over public spending, taxation, public services and Labour's electoral strategy. By the time of his departure, Starmer had become a significant figure in modern British political history. His biography therefore provides a contemporary account of a political career that included his transformation from human-rights lawyer and Director of Public Prosecutions into Labour leader and prime minister.

The Downing Street library has previously received books connected to prime ministers themselves, meaning Starmer's donation is not entirely without precedent. Political leaders have frequently left behind books, photographs, documents and other objects that help preserve the history of their time in office. What makes the latest addition particularly eye-catching is the combination of the book's subject and its author. Baldwin was not an outside historian writing decades later; he was a Labour adviser and political insider who had worked within Starmer's political operation. That connection gives the biography an unusually close perspective on Starmer's rise.

Baldwin's background is itself significant. Before becoming an author, he worked as a journalist and later served as an adviser within the Labour Party. His proximity to the party leadership means that the biography draws on a detailed understanding of the political environment surrounding Starmer's leadership. The book examines the Labour leader's attempt to reposition the party, rebuild its electoral coalition and move it toward a platform capable of winning a general election after the party's heavy defeat in 2019.

The donation also highlights the way political leaders become part of institutional history almost immediately after leaving office. Downing Street has been the workplace and residence of British prime ministers for centuries, and its library serves as an informal archive of political culture. Books donated by ministers and prime ministers can provide future historians with clues about what political figures considered important, influential or personally meaningful during their time in government.

There is also an element of political humour surrounding the decision. Donating a biography of oneself to an official government library is an unusual act and could easily be interpreted as self-important. Supporters, however, may see it more simply as part of the established tradition of outgoing political figures contributing books to the collection. The fact that the book was written by another person rather than being Starmer's own memoir also distinguishes it from a leader simply placing his personal political autobiography on the shelf.

The library's collection is particularly interesting because it reflects the personalities of different governments. Previous donations have ranged from political theory and historical biographies to poetry, religious works and books about hobbies. Such variety means the library functions as more than a collection of political literature. It provides a glimpse into the interests of the people who have occupied Downing Street and the intellectual influences surrounding British governments over the decades.

For Starmer, the biography's presence in Downing Street means that his political story will remain physically connected to the building where much of his premiership was conducted. Future visitors, officials and historians will be able to find the book among works left by earlier political figures. Its presence may ultimately become a small but memorable footnote in the history of the building.

The donation therefore carries significance beyond the novelty of a former prime minister giving a book about himself to an official library. It reflects the long-standing tradition of political leaders leaving behind books and objects that document their time in office. As Starmer's premiership becomes part of Britain's political history, Keir Starmer: The Biography will now occupy a place within the same Downing Street collection that has preserved traces of generations of British political leadership.
